forces: Concert band; arrangement by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: The United States Air Force Band plays Lawrence Odom’s arrangement of the Waltz of the Flowers, No. 13 from Act II of The Nutcracker, Op. 71. In this version brass and woodwind carry the long melodies over the three-beat dance.

relations.label: The principal waltz returns
relations.basis: The principal D-major waltz returns after the contrasting dance melodies. The first excerpt comes from its earlier restatement, and the later excerpt lies in the return marked near 302 s; both belong to the same principal group in Odom’s band arrangement. CENS diagonal mean 0.938, sustained 55 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 148.5 s (cache/form/tchaikovsky-waltz-flowers.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: United States Air Force Band recording, 1996
cues.text: The United States Air Force Band recorded this waltz for its 1996 album Christmas on Stage and Screen, where it is track 6. Lawrence Odom arranged Tchaikovsky’s orchestral score for the band’s brass and woodwind.
cues.evidence: The recording’s source credits Lawrence Odom and identifies track 6 of Christmas on Stage and Screen (1996). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Waltz_of_the_Flowers_-_Concert_Band_-_United_States_Air_Force_Band.mp3

cues.title: Harp cadenza
cues.text: The cadenza runs up and down through broken chords before the waltz begins in regular time. Tchaikovsky marks the solo ad libitum, and it ends on held chords.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson orchestral score, plate 17668, pp. 4–5: harp cadenza marked ad libitum, ending with held chords. The recording uses Lawrence Odom’s band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Waltz theme in D major
cues.text: The waltz begins in D major. A low first beat and two chords keep the triple metre while the melody runs across the bar lines. Shorter phrases follow each long phrase of the tune.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 5–6: D-major waltz accompaniment, horn melody and clarinet replies. This note describes the melody and accompaniment retained in the band version. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Vsevolozhsky, Rouen, 1891
cues.text: In Rouen in April 1891, Tchaikovsky asked Ivan Vsevolozhsky to postpone The Nutcracker and Iolanta. Given enough time, he promised “two masterpieces (pardon my immodesty)”. His ship for America was due to leave in two days, and the ballet was still unfinished.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Ivan Vsevolozhsky, letter 4363, Rouen, 3/15 April 1891. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=The_Nutcracker

cues.title: Middle section, B minor melody
cues.text: A high melody in short steps opens the middle section of the waltz. A longer tune follows, lower down, in B minor. Beneath both, the bass and offbeat chords keep to the three-beat pattern.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 14–17, rehearsal letters E–F: upper-wind tune followed by the B-minor viola-and-cello melody. The description follows the tunes, without assigning the original string parts to Odom’s band. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Suite première, Saint Petersburg, 1892
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducted the suite in Saint Petersburg on 19 March 1892, nine months before the ballet reached the stage. The waltz was the last number. Two days later he wrote to his publisher: “The suite from the ballet was successful.”
cues.evidence: Suite première 7/19 March 1892; Tchaikovsky to Pyotr Jurgenson, letter 4641, 9/21 March 1892. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/The_Nutcracker_(suite)

cues.title: Return of the principal waltz, D major
cues.text: At rehearsal H the principal waltz melodies return in D major. The three-beat accompaniment continues straight into the returning phrases, and there is no second cadenza.
cues.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 20 onwards, rehearsal H: return of the principal waltz group in D major. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chords in D major
cues.text: Repeated chords bring the waltz to its close in D major. The Waltz of the Flowers ends the concert suite. In the ballet the pas de deux follows it.
cues.evidence: Final D-major chords: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 35, https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624. Movement orders: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/The_Nutcracker_(suite) and https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=The_Nutcracker.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Ensemble chords lead to the cadenza
transitions.how: The introduction comes to rest on A, the dominant of D major. Sustained ensemble chords stop, and the soloist (the harp, in the original score) plays exposed broken chords, marked ad libitum. In this cadenza the soloist moves freely across the range of the instrument. The waltz then begins in a steady three beats to the bar.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson orchestral score, plate 17668, pp. 3–5. The solo is originally for harp; this recording is Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: The bass starts the waltz
transitions.to: A · Waltz theme in D major
transitions.how: The cadenza ends with held dominant chords. At the return to a tempo, D major arrives with a regular bass note on the first beat and chords on the next two. The horns then begin the long principal melody above this accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 5: held cadenza chords, a tempo accompaniment, then the D-major horn theme. Melodic and harmonic description for the band arrangement. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: Second tune in D major
transitions.from: A · Waltz theme in D major
transitions.to: B · High melody and lower B-minor melody
transitions.how: The principal group gives way to a high, lightly articulated tune in D major. The bass and offbeat chords continue underneath. A lower, more sustained melody follows in B minor, with rising runs above it.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, pp. 14–17, rehearsal E–F. The original upper-wind and lower-string tunes provide the melodic outline for this band-version note. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

transitions.title: Return of the waltz in D major
transitions.from: B · High melody and lower B-minor melody
transitions.to: A · Return of the D-major waltz
transitions.how: A descending bass line leads into the return of the principal waltz group in D major. The accompaniment continues in triple time, and the melody returns without the introductory cadenza. The score marks the returning tune cantabile.
transitions.evidence: Jurgenson score, plate 17668, p. 20, rehearsal H: descending bass link, D-major return and cantabile marking. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=22387&itemFileId=71624

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single unguarded melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
